title: Factors and Multiples Grade 4: The Simple Way to Tell Them Apart + Free Quiz
meta_title: Factors and Multiples Grade 4 Explained + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Factors and multiples grade 4 made simple: how to list all factors, spot prime vs composite, and stop the classic mix-up. Free 8-question quiz inside.
excerpt: Nine children out of ten muddle factors with multiples the first week. Here is the mental split that fixes it for good, plus how to list every factor of a number and a quick prime-or-composite check.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write the number 12 on a slip of paper, hand it to a Grade 4 child, and ask for its factors. Then ask for its multiples. Nine times out of ten the two lists come back swapped — or worse, blended into one confused jumble. This is the single stickiest muddle in the whole topic, and it is why factors and multiples grade 4 lessons live or die on one idea: knowing which word means ‘fits inside’ and which means ‘grows out of’. Get that split clear on day one and the rest is just careful listing.

Let me give you the plain-English version I use with my own students, then the systematic method, then the trap to watch for.

What a factor actually is

A factor of a number is a number that divides it exactly — no remainder, no leftover. If you can share 12 sweets equally among some children with none left over, the number of children is a factor of 12. So 3 is a factor of 12 (four sweets each), but 5 is not (12 ÷ 5 leaves 2 behind).

The second thing to teach, and the more powerful one, is that factors come in pairs. Every time you find one factor, you get its partner free. For 12: 1 pairs with 12, 2 pairs with 6, 3 pairs with 4. Three pairs, six factors, done. Thinking in pairs is what stops a child listing 1, 2, 3 and then giving up before they reach 6 and 12.

How to list ALL the factors of a number

Here is the method I drill until it is automatic. Work upward from 1, and for each number that divides exactly, write down both partners:

  • Start at 1. Does 1 divide 24? Always yes. Partner is 24. Write 1 and 24.
  • Try 2. 24 ÷ 2 = 12. Write 2 and 12.
  • Try 3. 24 ÷ 3 = 8. Write 3 and 8.
  • Try 4. 24 ÷ 4 = 6. Write 4 and 6.
  • Try 5. Does not divide exactly — skip it.
  • Try 6. But 6 already appeared as a partner of 4. Once your two numbers meet or cross, you have them all. Stop.

Factors of 24, in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Eight factors. The ‘stop when the pair meets’ rule is the bit textbooks often leave out, and it is exactly what saves a child from checking 7, 9, 10, 11 and 13 for no reason.

What a multiple actually is

A multiple of a number is simply its times-table, stretched out as far as you like. The multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 … and they never stop. You get them by multiplying 4 by 1, then 2, then 3, and onward forever. If factors are about dividing, multiples are about multiplying — that opposite is worth saying out loud.

A quick sanity check children enjoy: 12 is a multiple of 4, AND 4 is a factor of 12. Same relationship, read from two ends. Once a child sees that ‘4 is a factor of 12’ and ‘12 is a multiple of 4’ describe the very same fact, the fog usually lifts.

The difference students always confuse

This is the heart of it, so I make it a rule they can chant. Factors are few, and they are never bigger than the number. Multiples are endless, and they are never smaller than the number.

 Factors of a numberMultiples of a number
Found byDividing (what fits in)Multiplying (times-table)
How manyA small, finite listEndless
SizeLess than or equal to the numberGreater than or equal to the number
Smallest oneAlways 1The number itself
Example for 61, 2, 3, 66, 12, 18, 24, 30 …

Notice the number itself sits in both lists: 6 is the largest factor of 6 and the smallest multiple of 6. That overlap confuses some children, so I point it out before they trip over it rather than after.

A gentle first look at prime and composite numbers

Once factors are solid, prime versus composite falls out naturally — it is just a factor-count in disguise. A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. A composite number has more than two. So 7 is prime (only 1 and 7 divide it), while 8 is composite (1, 2, 4 and 8).

One honest caveat that trips up even good students, and adults: 1 is neither prime nor composite. It has only a single factor — itself — so it fails the ‘exactly two’ test for prime. Do not let a child file 1 under prime; it is a special case, full stop.

A counter-intuitive nudge worth planting early: 2 is the only even prime number. Every other even number has 2 as a factor, which instantly gives it a third factor and makes it composite. Children find it oddly satisfying that 2 is the lone exception.

A quick practice routine that sticks

Ten minutes beats an hour. Pick a number under 30 each day and have the child do three things: list all its factors in pairs, write its first five multiples, then say whether it is prime or composite. Rotate the number daily. Within a fortnight the pairing method and the ‘few and small versus endless and big’ rule become second nature.

quiz.title: Grade 4 Factors and Multiples Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on factors, multiples, and prime versus composite numbers. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 4 factors, multiples, prime and composite

questions.q: Which of these is a factor of 12?
questions.explanation: 12 divided by 4 is 3 with no remainder, so 4 is a factor. 5, 8 and 7 all leave a remainder.

questions.q: What are ALL the factors of 10?
questions.explanation: Work in pairs: 1 and 10, then 2 and 5. That gives 1, 2, 5, 10 - four factors in all.

questions.q: Which number is a multiple of 6?
questions.explanation: The multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and so on. 24 is 6 times 4.

options: A factor is bigger than the number
A multiple is never smaller than the number
1 is not a factor of any number
questions.explanation: Multiples start at the number itself and grow, so a multiple is never smaller than the number. Factors, by contrast, are never bigger than it.

questions.q: Which of these is a prime number?
questions.explanation: 13 has exactly two factors, 1 and 13, so it is prime. 9, 15 and 21 each have more than two factors.

options: It has more than two factors
questions.explanation: 8 has the factors 1, 2, 4 and 8 - more than two - so it is composite. Being even is not the reason on its own.
7 divides exactly only by 1 and 7, so it has exactly two factors, which makes it prime.

questions.q: Which number is neither prime nor composite?
questions.explanation: 1 has only a single factor, itself, so it fails the 'exactly two factors' test for prime and is not composite either. It is a special case.

faq.q: What is the difference between a factor and a multiple?
faq.a: A factor divides a number exactly and is never larger than it — the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. A multiple is the number’s times-table and is never smaller than it — the multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36 and so on, endlessly. Factors are few; multiples are infinite.

faq.q: How do I list all the factors of a number without missing any?
faq.a: Work upward from 1 in pairs. For each number that divides exactly, write both it and its partner (for 18: 1 and 18, 2 and 9, 3 and 6). Stop as soon as the two numbers in a pair meet or cross — you have found them all.
No. A prime number needs exactly two factors, but 1 has only one factor (itself). So 1 is neither prime nor composite — it is a special case that sits outside both groups.

faq.q: What is the smallest prime number, and is any even number prime?
faq.a: The smallest prime is 2, and it is the only even prime. Every other even number has 2 as a factor, which gives it a third factor and makes it composite.
